newsitem.title: USA: Gloomy weather hurt retail sales in May, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Gloomy weather hurt retail sales in May, experts say.

text.p: Gloomy weather put a damper on the retail trade in May, and large store chains are expected to post soft sales results for the month, experts said Tuesday.
Floods and low temperatures swept many markets, and big store chains were left holding large inventories of outdoor equipment, summer clothing and gardening products.

TeleCheck Services Inc., which tracked spending by consumers who wrote checks for purchases at 27,000 retail locations, said May sales rose 2.3 percent from a year ago vs. an increase of 2.1 percent in May 1996.

Despite the slight increase, the survey showed economic growth has slowed from the rapid clip of the first quarter when the economy expanded by 5.8 percent, said William Ford, an economist with TeleCheck.
Consumers "are being pretty careful about how they're spending money," Ford said. "The retailers are probably not overjoyed with these numbers."
Major retailers are scheduled to report sales results for May on Thursday.
Two of the nation's largest retailers -- Sears, Roebuck & Co. and Kmart Corp. -- are expected to report sales either dropped or were weaker than expected.
Merrill Lynch & Co. estimated that same-store sales -- by stores open for at least a year -- rose by 2.5 percent last month vs. 3.8 percent in May of 1996.

The swollen inventories at many chains have raised a red flag about future clearance sales, which could pull down earnings for the industry in the second quarter if demand doesn't pick up, analysts said.

"They just may lose the seasonal business altogether," said Michael Exstein (eds: correct spelling) of Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "You just get to the point where you don't buy an air conditioner."
Consumers went on a buying spree earlier this year, but purchasing began to slow in April. Some experts said spending may not pick up again until the fall.

A NatWest Securities Corp. research report said same-store sales rose 3.8 percent in February, March and April combined and forecast an increase of 2.1 percent for May. Business may not pick up again until new fashions hit the stores, leaving summer goods to collect dust on store shelves.
Wal-Mart, the nation's largest retailer, is expected to report same-store sales rose about 3.0 percent, analysts said.
Sales at Sears fell about 2 percent, they said. Kmart's sales rose about 2.5 percent to 3.0 percent, below the Chicago-based company's expectations.

Dayton Hudson Corp., parent of Target discount stores, is expected to post a 4.0 percent rise, and Federated Department Stores Inc., parent of Bloomingdale's and Macy's, saw an increase of about 2.0 percent during May, analysts said.
